food.text: The Gunditjmara people engineered an extensive system of aquaculture using wetlands created by lava flows from the Budj Bim volcano. They built stone channels, ponds and traps to farm short-finned eels for food.
On the coast near Gunditjmara Country, other clans ate a rich fish diet. According to an early colonist, this diet also included whale flesh, known in their language as cunderbul.

Across more than 100 square kilometres of their Country, the Gunditjmara built stone channels, traps and canals. These structures were used to catch short-finned eels, called kooyang, which were the staple of their diet.

Indigenous Australians have lived in Australia for some 65,000 years. In that time they developed a unique hunter-gatherer diet, known as bush tucker, drawn from regional Australian plants and animals.
Aboriginal Tasmanians foraged native edibles, known as bush tucker, which they also used for other purposes such as construction. Tasmania has no crops like maize grown for large production.

At Lake Condah, part of the Budj Bim wetlands, the Kerrup Gunditj clan engineered an extensive aquaculture system. Other Gunditjmara clans worked with them to establish eel trapping and farming, and to develop smoking techniques to preserve the harvest.

Between about 18,000 and 7,000 years ago, many societies around the world took up agriculture. In Australia, environmental change did not lead to farming, and people carried on as hunters and gatherers.

Wombat meat was a source of bush food from the arrival of Aboriginal Australians until the arrival of Europeans. Wombats thrive in eastern Australia and Tasmania, and wombat stew was once one of the few truly Australian dishes.
To preserve their catch, the Gunditjmara smoked kooyang, the short-finned eels central to their diet. They used burning leaves from the Australian blackwood tree for the smoking.
Some of the stone groundwork the Gunditjmara built for their eel-trapping system is older than the Egyptian pyramids. This comparison shows just how ancient this food-producing engineering is.

The broadening of the Australian diet was linked to climatic changes, including the sea level rises of the Flandrian transgression. As the climate shifted, foragers relied on more kinds of food, including fish, water fowl and shellfish.
The manna of the cider gum (Eucalyptus gunnii) was used by Aboriginal Tasmanians to make a syrup or an alcohol, a kind of cider. It is one of the island's unusual foraged trees.
Tasmanian wattles such as blackwood (Acacia melanoxylon) and mimosa (Acacia dealbata) could have their seeds eaten. The seeds could also be crushed into a powder.

Archaeologist Heather Builth argued that the Gunditjmara built stone dams in the swampy volcanic areas of the Budj Bim lava flow. This created ponds and wetlands that formed a sophisticated system of aquaculture and eel farming.

Tasmania's bush tucker also included berries such as snowberry (Gaultheria hispida), fruits such as heartberry (Aristotelia peduncularis), and vegetables such as river mint (Mentha australis). All of these were foraged rather than farmed.

art.text: In northwest Arnhem Land, researchers documented 572 paintings at 87 sites, known as the Maliwawa Figures. They are estimated to have been made between 6,000 and 9,400 years ago. The figures are large and unusually show relationships between people and animals, a rare theme in rock art.

Many thousands of Aboriginal engravings are known around Sydney, carved into Sydney sandstone as carefully drawn people, animals and symbols. They date to around 5,000 years, with some possibly as old as 7,000 years. The style is quite unlike rock art found anywhere else in Australia.

The Maliwawa paintings include bilbies and the first known depiction of a dugong. Bilbies are not known historically in Arnhem Land, and bilbies, thylacines and dugong have been extinct there for millennia. The art is naturalistic and painted in red to mulberry colours.

The locations of most Sydney rock engravings are not publicised, to prevent damage by vandalism and to retain their sanctity. Aboriginal Australians still regard them as sacred sites. They are found mainly in Ku-ring-gai Council, Sydney Harbour and the Blue Mountains.

The Maliwawa Figures were first seen by researchers in 2008-2009, but were only studied in field research lasting from 2016 to 2018. The study, led by Paul Taçon, was published in Australian Archaeology in September 2020. The figures were named by Ronald Lamilami, a senior traditional owner.

Paul Taçon says the Maliwawa back-to-back figures are the oldest known for western Arnhem Land. It appears this painting convention began with the Maliwawa style. He says it continues to the present with bark paintings and paintings on paper.

Sydney's engravings cannot be dated straightforwardly, so archaeologists use indirect dating. Those in a style called simple figurative are dated to around 3,000 BC and 4,000 BC. The picture is complicated because engravings were sometimes re-grooved during ceremonies.

Paul Taçon compared the Maliwawa Figures with George Chaloupka's Dynamic Figures style. In the Dynamic Figures, about 89 percent of the subjects are humans, compared with 42% of the Maliwawa Figures. The article notes there is much complexity and debate about classifying Arnhem Land rock art styles.

war.text: The oldest surviving Aboriginal boomerang, held today in the South Australian Museum, was found in a peat bog in South Australia and has been dated to 10,000 BC, right at the start of this era. It shows Aboriginal Australians were already crafting refined hunting weapons this early.

Wooden javelins and boomerangs made by Aboriginal Australians have been found dating from around 10,000 years ago. This was part of a wave of new technologies that emerged in Australia as the climate grew warmer during this era.

In the Kimberley, the most recent Gwion Gwion rock art tradition, the Clothes Peg style, includes at least one panel showing a battle, with two ranks of opponents lined up facing each other. Most Gwion Gwion figures are estimated to have been painted around 12,000 years ago.

Stone points made specifically for spears appear in the Australian record from about 5,000 to 7,000 years ago, a more specialised weapon than the earlier wooden javelins and boomerangs. This reflects a broader shift toward new stone-tool technologies during this era.

Sea levels around Australia stabilised close to their current level about 6,500 years ago. Spear-throwers were probably developed only some time after that point, making them one of the last major weapons advances to appear before the end of this era.

The Clothes Peg Gwion Gwion figures, the artists' most recent style, are shown holding multi-barbed spears, spear-throwers and woven bags, often in aggressive stances. Unlike earlier Gwion Gwion styles, fine anatomical detail such as their waists and feet is missing from these figures.

The woomera, a wooden spear-throwing device similar to the atlatl, is recorded as having been used in Australia from about 5,000 years ago. Held in one hand, it let a spear travel at far greater speed and force than a hand-thrown spear alone could achieve.

Non-returning boomerangs, sometimes called throwsticks or kylies, were used to hunt prey ranging from kangaroos to parrots. At a range of about 100 metres, a 2-kilogram non-returning boomerang could inflict mortal injury on a large animal. Kylies were typically much larger than returning boomerangs and flew in straight lines, and because of their size and hook shapes they could cripple or kill an animal or a human opponent. Medium-weight ones were sometimes thrown at the enemy in close-quarters fights, and recent evidence suggests boomerangs were used as war weapons.

Between about 8,000 and 6,000 years ago, rising seas flooded coastlines and formed thousands of islands around Australia, including in the Torres Strait. The historian Josephine Flood suggests this loss of land pushed Aboriginal groups toward stronger territorial boundaries and sharper clan identity.

Many woomeras also carried a sharp stone cutting edge, called a tula adze, fixed to the handle with gum from the triodia plant. This turned the spear-throwing weapon into a multi-purpose tool that could also cut up game or wood.

science.text: The Ghow Swamp site in the North Central region of Victoria holds the largest known single population of human skeletal remains from the late Pleistocene. The remains date from between 13,000 and 9,300 years ago and lie in the lunette on the eastern rim of a former wetland near the Murray River.

Early scientific descriptions of the Ghow Swamp skulls noted massive brow regions and a receding forehead. They were taken to preserve an almost unmodified eastern erectus form. The features were read as the survival of Homo erectus features in Australia until as recently as 10,000 years ago.

In Australia, environmental change between roughly 18,000 and 7,000 years ago did not give rise to agriculture, unlike in many Neolithic societies elsewhere in the world. Archaeologists suggest the change may instead have contributed to the disappearance of animal populations already made vulnerable by hunting.

Alan Thorne carried out archaeological excavations at Ghow Swamp between 1968 and 1972 on behalf of the Australian National University. His work recovered the partial skeletal remains of more than 22 individuals from the site, which is 10 kilometres south-east of Cohuna.

Donald Brothwell disputed the idea that the Ghow Swamp skulls showed surviving Homo erectus features. He suggested that the vault size and shape had been influenced by artificial cranial deformation, particularly in Kow Swamp 5.
Further remains were found around Ghow Swamp by an interested local resident, Gordon Spark. By 1972 the remains of at least forty individuals had been excavated and studied.

Between the 1960s and early 1980s, Victorian Government agencies approved the excavation of human remains at Ghow Swamp without seeking the consent of the Traditional Owners. Authorities claimed the excavations would advance science, and the finds were interpreted as representing different waves of immigrants to Australia before European discovery. It was later argued that the studies provided very little scientific gain, and the concerns raised by the Aboriginal community were either ignored or dismissed.

culture.text: In northwest Arnhem Land, researchers documented 572 paintings across 87 sites, now called the Maliwawa Figures. They are estimated to have been drawn between 6,000 and 9,400 years ago, in red to mulberry colours and a naturalistic style.

Around Sydney, Aboriginal artists carved careful images of people, animals and symbols into sandstone. Dating to around 5,000 years, with some possibly as old as 7,000 years, they are found mainly in Ku-ring-gai, Sydney Harbour and the Blue Mountains.
Wooden javelins and boomerangs have been found in Australia dating from 10,000 years ago. Spear throwers were probably developed more recently, within the last 6,500 years.

Some Sydney engraving sites may have been increase sites, where a ceremony was held to increase the availability of a food source such as kangaroos or fish. Most sites depicting animals are thought to be of this type.

From about 6,500 years ago, elaborate fish and eel traps with channels up to three kilometres long were in use in western Victoria. Around the same time, semi-permanent collections of wooden huts on mounds appeared there, linked to more systematic use of wetland food sources.

The Maliwawa art was first seen by researchers in 2008-2009, but was only studied in field research from 2016 to 2018. Senior traditional owner Ronald Lamilami named the figures, and Paul Taçon led the study published in September 2020.

Some Sydney engravings may mark initiation sites, where a young boy's transition into manhood was celebrated. The lines of steps, called mundoes, may indicate the ceremonial path from childhood into manhood.

Sydney's engravings of the "simple figurative" style are dated to around 3,000 BC and 4,000 BC, and they cannot be dated directly. Dating is complicated because the engravings were sometimes "re-grooved" during ceremonies.
The Maliwawa Figures differ from George Chaloupka's Dynamic Figures style. About 89 percent of the subjects in the Dynamic Figures are humans, compared with 42% in the Maliwawa Figures.
Some Sydney engravings show Ancestral Beings. Baiame has a striped head-dress and often a striped body, while Daramulan has a large club foot and may have been part-emu.
